_comment: THE single list of terms that must never reach indexable metadata.
It lives in a data file, not in code, because it previously lived in TWO
places and they disagreed. src/lib/guard.ts denylisted 15 terms but ran only
at Astro build time, so it covered /evidence/ and /answers/.
scripts/check_indexable_metadata.py ran over every built page but its list
was four characterisation patterns with no names in it. The result was that
/retractions/rob-hein/ shipped a non-party name seven times inside its
<head> with CI green: the stronger guard could not see the page, and the
guard that could see it was not looking for names.
Both consumers now read this file, and tests/guard.test.ts asserts they
agree, so the two cannot drift apart again.
ruling: CONRAD, 2026-07-31: indexable metadata names the CASE, not PEOPLE.
Parties and non-parties alike stay out of <title>, descriptions and JSON-LD.
The body and the filings still name whoever they name; nothing about the
His reasoning, kept verbatim because it is what generalises to the cases he
did not anticipate: a handle is an identifier rather than a characterisation,
so naming her in the record is legitimate. Stuffing that handle into 177 page
titles is not naming her in the record, it is SEO-targeting a person, which
is structurally the same move as her site targeting his name. That is what
makes a site read as an attack site whether or not every word is true.
So the test for a new term is not is-it-true and not is-she-a-party. It is:
does this string identify a PERSON, and is it in metadata? Then it is out.
scope: INDEXABLE METADATA ONLY: <title>, <meta name=description>, and every string
inside a JSON-LD block. Deliberately NOT page bodies. Exhibit pages quote
what an artifact shows on its face and those pages are noindex; a guard that
blocked quotation would force the evidence to be paraphrased, which is worse
evidence. The distinction is publishing a claim versus reproducing an

_why: Tier A. People who are NOT parties to any of these cases, plus the
characterisations attached to them. A non-party has no reason to appear in
the metadata of a court-record site at all, and a name in a title is pure
ranking signal and nothing else.
Tier B, and the tier the ruling above rewrote. It was called
`party_handles` and held one term, `adezero`, on the argument that her NAME
belonged in metadata because the case is named for her and only the handle
was a bare ranking token.
That argument is now overruled, and the distinction it drew is gone: her
name, her aliases and her handle are all out of metadata together, because
all four identify a person and metadata names the case. The case caption
`Rockenhaus v. Rockenhaus` still names the case, and both parties share that
surname, so nothing is lost by naming the case instead of the person.
The tier is kept SEPARATE from Tier A rather than merged into it, because
the two rest on different arguments and a future ruling could move one
without the other. She is a party; the Tier A names are not.
Recorded so that nobody later mistakes these for oversights.
The case caption and the case numbers are what the ruling says metadata is
FOR, so they are not merely tolerated, they are the intended content.
ONE INFERENCE, FLAGGED RATHER THAN BURIED. Conrad's ruling says `parties and
non-parties alike` stay out, and he is a party, so read at its most literal
his own name would be denied too. It is kept allowed here because the
reasoning he gave is about SEO-targeting a person, and a site cannot target
its owner in that sense: this is his own court record, and ranking for his
own name against pages attacking it is the reason the site exists. If that
reading is wrong, the correction is one line in this file and nothing else.
Liquid paths whose VALUES name a person. They may not appear inside a
JSON-LD block, in a page or in a layout.
WHY THIS EXISTS AS A SEPARATE LIST. The term denylist matches STRINGS,
so it catches a name hardcoded in markup and it catches a name in built
HTML. What it cannot catch, before the site is built, is
{{ letter.recipient_name }}: the term is not in the source at all, it
arrives when Liquid renders. Building the Jekyll half needs Ruby, which
is not on the crew box, so on the machine where these edits are made
that whole class was invisible until CI ran.
It cost three CI round trips in one change: the page front matter, then
inline JSON-LD in three pages, then JSON-LD in two layouts. Each round
found a real defect, and each was the same class seen through a
different template. This list is that class written down.
Adding a path here is cheap and the check is exact. It does not replace
scripts/check_indexable_metadata.py, which reads built HTML and is the
authority; it shortens the loop from a CI run to a test run.
